messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Daniel had always understood his work as a military medic in practical terms: keep moving, keep triaging, keep your hands steady when other people are losing control. That sense of purpose had given shape to his life, especially after his wife died three years earlier, leaving him widowed and accustomed to carrying grief quietly alongside duty. The traumatic event that brought him to treatment had happened during a domestic disaster response deployment after a powerful hurricane tore through a coastal town where units were helping with search, evacuation, and emergency medical care. Daniel was in a school gymnasium turned temporary shelter when the roof began to fail under wind and water damage. He later described the moment in fragments: a crack overhead, a blast of shouting, folding chairs scraping, then darkness and the sound of people crying out. A section of the ceiling gave way and water flooded across the floor. He was trying to reach an older woman who had fallen when the noise and chaos escalated, and he remembered feeling the same raw terror he felt in the moment as he recalled it afterward. What made the scene so hard to hold together in his mind was that the memory did not come back in a neat sequence; even now he struggled to put the event in the right order, starting with the collapse, then jumping to the screaming, then to his own body hitting the floor, then to the desperate attempt to get others moving toward the exits. He could not tell the story without stopping, because when he pictured it in detail he became so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to pause, look away, or rub his face until he could continue.

In the weeks after the deployment, Daniel noticed that loud or unexpected sounds landed in him with a jolt that was out of proportion to the present moment. A dropped pan in the kitchen, a door slamming in the apartment hallway, a truck backfiring outside the grocery store, even a sudden burst of static from the radio in his work vehicle could pull him instantly into a state of alarm. He became highly alert to noise, scanning for what might come next, and he found himself unable to settle even in places he knew were safe, including his own home after he returned from the assignment. He sat with his shoulders tight, eyes moving to windows, exits, and overhead fixtures without thinking about it. At work, where he still served as a medic, the ordinary sounds of the base and field environment kept him on edge in a way that embarrassed him because he knew his surroundings were not dangerous in the same way as the hurricane response scene. Still, he remained watchful, with a constant sense that he needed to be ready for the next sudden sound or sign that things were about to go wrong. He began sleeping lightly and staying tense through the day, saying that relaxation no longer felt available to him even when nothing around him was threatening.

Over time, Daniel also found that reminders of the disaster brought the memory back with a force that felt immediate rather than distant. When a storm warning was mentioned on the news, or when he heard heavy rain striking metal surfaces, he felt his body react as if he were back in the collapsing shelter. The same was true when he encountered certain sounds during his hospital shifts or on base, especially abrupt bangs or clattering that echoed through hallways and workspaces. At those moments he did not merely remember the event; he relived the fear of it, and the emotional surge was so intense that he often had to stop what he was doing and collect himself before continuing. He noticed that the memory came in pieces, not as a full story but as disconnected flashes, which left him unsettled and frustrated because he could not make the experience fit into a coherent account of what had happened. He was troubled not only by the terror itself but by what the terror seemed to say about him. The beliefs that had once organized his life no longer held in the same way. He had come to feel that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, and this loss of meaning was particularly painful because his work had once given him identity and direction. He now described feeling as if he did not know himself anymore, as though the man who had been steady in crises, useful to others, and certain of his place in the world had been replaced by someone more frightened and less recognizable. More broadly, his beliefs about how the world worked felt completely destroyed. The hurricane response had shown him, in his mind, that stability could vanish without warning and that structures meant to protect people could fail in a moment.

By the time he sought help, Daniel was not coming in because of a single dramatic worsening but because the accumulation had become impossible to ignore. He had started avoiding the most obvious reminders by turning off news coverage during storm season and keeping himself busy during weather alerts, yet the larger problem was that he no longer felt able to trust ordinary moments. He wanted to be able to stand in a room without tracking every sound, and he wanted to return to the kind of steadiness his job demanded. What finally brought him in was the worry that he was becoming a stranger to himself and that this sense of emptiness and disconnection might become permanent. He said he was not sure what he expected therapy to do, but he hoped it might help him find some way to live with the memory without being knocked over by it each time it returned, and without feeling as though the world, and his own life in it, had lost their meaning.
